title: Bash Scripting Quiz
description: Write safer shell scripts: strict mode, quoting, exit codes, functions, traps, arrays, and process substitution through real-world DevOps scenarios

questions.title: Strict Mode
questions.description: What does `set -euo pipefail` at the top of a bash script do?
questions.situation: You're writing a deploy script and want it to fail fast instead of silently continuing after an error.
questions.codeExample:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

./build.sh
./deploy.sh   # should NOT run if build.sh fails
options: Enables strict mode: exit on any error, treat unset variables as errors, and fail a pipeline if any command in it fails
Turns on debug tracing so every command is printed before it runs
Runs the script with elevated (root) privileges
Forces the script to use UTF-8 encoding for all string operations
questions.explanation: `set -euo pipefail` combines three safeguards: `-e` exits immediately if a command fails, `-u` errors on unset variables (catching typos like $SEREVR), and `-o pipefail` makes a pipeline return the first failing command's status instead of only the last one's. Together they turn silent failures into loud, early ones.
questions.hint: Each letter is a separate shell option. Think about what -e, -u, and pipefail each guard against.

questions.title: Quoting Variables
questions.description: Why should you write `"$filename"` instead of `$filename`?
questions.situation: Your backup script works fine until someone creates a file named "my report.txt" - then it breaks.
options: Unquoted variables are split on whitespace and expanded as globs, so "my report.txt" becomes two arguments
Quoted variables run faster because bash skips parsing them
Unquoted variables are treated as integers by cp
There is no difference; quoting is just a style preference
questions.explanation: Without quotes, bash performs word splitting (on spaces, tabs, newlines) and pathname expansion (globbing with * and ?) on the variable's value. `"my report.txt"` unquoted becomes two arguments (`my` and `report.txt`), and a value like `*.log` would expand to matching filenames. Double quotes suppress both, passing the value through exactly.
questions.hint: Think about what bash does to unquoted text before the command ever sees it.

questions.title: Checking Success
questions.description: How do you check whether the previous command succeeded?
questions.situation: Your script runs a database migration and must stop if the migration fails.
options: Test `$?` - it holds the previous command's exit status, and 0 means success
Test `$#` - it holds the previous command's exit status
Test `$!` - it holds the previous command's exit status
Check `$0` - it is set to "success" or "failure"
questions.explanation: `$?` expands to the exit status of the most recently executed command. By convention 0 means success and anything else (1-255) signals an error. `$#` is the argument count, `$!` is the last background PID, and `$0` is the script name - none of them carry status info.
questions.hint: One of these special variables is documented as 'the exit status of the most recently executed foreground pipeline'.

questions.title: Test Brackets
questions.description: What is the practical advantage of `[[ ]]` over `[ ]` in conditionals?
questions.situation: You need to check whether a filename matches a pattern like `*.tar.gz` inside an if statement.
options: [[ ]] supports pattern matching with ==, prevents word splitting, and allows && / || inside the test
[[ ]] runs the test in a subshell so it is faster
[[ ]] works in sh (POSIX shell) while [ ] is bash-only
There is no difference; [[ ]] is just newer syntax for the same test command
questions.explanation: `[[ ]]` is a bash keyword (not the external `[`/`test` command), so it gets special parsing: `==` does glob pattern matching, variables aren't word-split inside it, and you can use `&&`/`||` directly. It's actually the reverse of option 2: `[[ ]]` is bash/ksh/zsh-only, while `[ ]` is the POSIX-portable form.
questions.hint: One of these is parsed specially by the shell itself rather than run as a command.

questions.title: Function Scope
questions.description: Why should you declare variables as `local` inside bash functions?
questions.situation: Two functions in your script both use a variable named `count`, and values are leaking between them.
options: Without local, every variable in bash is global - assignments inside functions overwrite same-named variables everywhere
local makes the variable read-only so functions can't change it
local variables are stored in a faster memory region
local is required for the function to return a value with echo
questions.explanation: Bash has no block scope and function variables default to global scope. An assignment like `count=5` inside a function silently overwrites any global `count`. Declaring `local count` confines the variable to the function (and its children), preventing spooky action-at-a-distance bugs when functions share common names like `i`, `file`, or `count`.
questions.hint: Bash functions don't get their own scope unless you ask for it.

questions.title: Cleanup on Exit
questions.description: How do you guarantee a temp file is removed even if your script errors out halfway?
questions.situation: Your script creates /tmp/work.$$ files. When it fails, the temp files pile up on the server.
questions.codeExample:
tmp=$(mktemp)
trap 'rm -f "$tmp"' EXIT
# ... rest of script ...
options: Register a trap on EXIT - bash runs it whenever the shell exits, for any reason
Add `rm -f "$tmp"` as the very last line of the script
Run the script with `bash --clean-tmp`
Temp files in /tmp are always auto-deleted when a script exits
questions.explanation: `trap 'cmd' EXIT` registers a handler that bash executes on any shell exit - normal completion, an error under `set -e`, or a signal like SIGINT/SIGTERM. A `rm` on the last line never runs if the script dies early, there is no `--clean-tmp` flag, and /tmp cleanup is the OS's job on its own schedule, not the script's.
questions.hint: You need something that runs no matter HOW the script ends.

questions.title: Default Values
questions.description: What is the difference between `${PORT-default}` and `${PORT:-default}`?
questions.situation: Your script reads an optional PORT env var. It should fall back to 8080 when PORT is unset OR empty.
options: The colon form also treats an empty string as missing; without the colon only a truly unset variable triggers the default
The colon form is slower but more portable across shells
Without the colon, the default is only a warning and PORT stays empty
There is no difference; the colon is optional decoration
questions.explanation: In `${var-word}` the default applies only when `var` is unset. In `${var:-word}` (with colon) it applies when `var` is unset OR null (empty). Since `PORT=""` is set-but-empty, only the colon form falls back to 8080. This distinction matters whenever an env var might be explicitly emptied, which is common in CI environments.
questions.hint: One form cares about empty strings, the other only about unset variables.

questions.title: Array Expansion
questions.description: Why should you expand bash arrays as `"${files[@]}"` and not `$files` or `${files[*]}`?
questions.situation: You're looping over filenames that may contain spaces, stored in an array.
questions.codeExample:
files=("a.txt" "my report.txt")
for f in "${files[@]}"; do
  echo "processing: $f"
done
options: "${files[@]}" expands to each element as a separate quoted word; $files gives only the first element and ${files[*]} joins everything into one string
"${files[@]}" sorts the array alphabetically before expanding
There is no difference once the array is quoted
${files[*]} is the correct form; [@] is deprecated
questions.explanation: `$files` (or `${files}`) is shorthand for `${files[0]}` - just the first element. `"${files[*]}"` joins all elements into a single word (with the first char of IFS), breaking on spaces. Only `"${files[@]}"` expands to N separately-quoted words, preserving elements that contain spaces. This is the single most common bash array bug.
questions.hint: Try each form with an element that contains a space and count the resulting words.

questions.title: Process Substitution
questions.description: When is `<(command)` (process substitution) the right tool?
questions.situation: You need to diff the sorted contents of two files without creating intermediate temp files.
options: When a command needs filenames but you want to feed it command output - bash substitutes a /dev/fd path carrying the live output
When you want to run a command in the background and continue immediately
It is identical to $(command); the angle bracket is just an alias
When you need to redirect a command's stderr to a log file
questions.explanation: `<(cmd)` runs the command with its output attached to a file descriptor (like /dev/fd/63), and that path is substituted into the command line. Tools like `diff` that insist on file arguments - not stdin - can then read live command output as if it were a file. `$( )` captures output as a string instead, which can't stream and breaks on large/binary data.
questions.hint: diff wants files, not strings. How do you give it 'files' that are actually command output?

questions.title: Pipeline Failures
questions.description: In `false | true`, `$?` is 0. How do you detect that the FIRST command failed?
questions.situation: Your CI step runs `generate-report | upload-report`. Uploads succeed but reports are empty - the generator is failing silently.
questions.codeExample:
set -o pipefail
generate-report | upload-report
echo "generator: ${PIPESTATUS[0]}, uploader: ${PIPESTATUS[1]}"
options: Use the PIPESTATUS array - it holds each pipeline command's exit code; also enable `set -o pipefail` so the pipeline itself reports failure
Use `$?` twice in a row - the second read gives the first command's status
Pipelines always report the first failure, so `$?` is enough
Store the output in a variable first, then check `$?`
questions.explanation: A pipeline's `$?` is only the LAST command's status, so `false | true` looks successful. `${PIPESTATUS[0]}` gives the first command's code (bash sets this array after every pipeline). And `set -o pipefail` makes the pipeline return the rightmost non-zero status, so `set -e` scripts actually stop on mid-pipeline failures instead of sailing past them.
questions.hint: The shell remembers every command's status in a pipeline - just not in $?.
